Abdul Quayum, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner.

Arshed Ali Sikder (Md) ------ Petitioner 
vs 
Gouranga Chandra Shil and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment: 6. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the lower appellate Court committed an error of law in its decision occasioning failure of justice in reversing the judgment of the trial Court without reversing its finding on record. He also submits that the trial Court found the agreement is not a genuine one which is created for the purpose of the case and was ante-dated. He also points out that the original agreement was not filed before the trial Court and the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 reveal that photocopy of the same was filed only, but the lower appellate Court by the order dated 19-10-94 without appreciating that the original document was not filed in the trial Court and the plaintiff collusively entered the same in the list of documents and sent the record to the trial Court for preparing exhibit list and for marking the papers proved in evidence and soon after that the petitioner as respondent filed an application for vacating the said order which was rejected by the lower appellate Court without assigning any reason. The trial Court instead of the photocopy sent the original agreement, which was not proved in evidence, to the lower appellate Court marking it as Exhibit 1. He also submits that the finding of the trial Court to the effect that the agreement is not genuine, particularly because of the evidence of the PWs as to purchase of the stamp used in the agreement are contradictory and discrepant showing the document ante-dated and forged was not reversed by the lower appellate Court in his judgment of reversal and thus it is not a proper judgment of reversal. In support of his contention the learned Lawyer refers a decision as reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 229. The learned Lawyer next submits that the appellate Court found that the agreement contains the signatures of the attesting witnesses of the Kabala and the signatures of both the documents are common, but actually the scribe did not depose and his affidavit Exhibit 5 is not an evidence and the agreement was not proved nor even filed in the trial Court and PWs 1, 2 and 3 only referred to and proved a photocopy and there was no explanation why the photocopy was proved in .evidence and under section 63 of the Evidence Act one is bound to give explanation for producing secondary evidence, and without such explanation it cannot go into evidence. In support of his contention the learned Lawyer refers to a decision as reported in 47 DLR (AD) 45 wherein their Lordships held that a party producing secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution of the original and even where a document is exhibited without objection, the Court is to be satisfied as to its execution. The learned Lawyer submits that the original agreement was not proved in evidence. The learned Lawyer submits that ante-dating of documents constitutes the offence of forgery as per the illustrations cited in section 464 of the Penal Code. In support of his contention the learned Lawyer refers a decision as reported in 2 BCR 84. The learned Lawyer next submits that the petitioner is not a party to the agreement and the contract is not binding on him unless it can be proved that the transfer is collusive and the lower appellate Court decreed the suit without considering this aspect. The Learned Lawyer also submits that it is true that the High Court Division cannot interfere with the findings of fact by the last Court of fact but it can interfere if the interference is being based on detecting error apparent on the face of the record resulting in the failure of justice. In support of his contention, the learned Lawyer has referred a decision as reported in 51 DLR (AD) 55. The learned Lawyer points out that there is clear violation of Order XIII, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides as to how a document admitted in evidence should be endorsed and marked as exhibit. He also refers to Rules 396 and 403 of CRO and paragraph 26(8) of Civil Suit Instruction Manual and submits that the mandatory provisions of law have not been complied with, he submits that if the exhibits are not properly marked and if there is no order by the trial Court admitting the same as evidence and marking them as exhibits, those documents cannot be relied upon by the Court of appeal. In support of his contention he has referred a decision as reported in 9 BLC 333. Lastly, Lawyer for the petitioner submits that the judgment of the lower appellate Court suffers from illegality which is not sustainable in law and, as such, is liable to be set aside.
